title: CAN YOU DEFEND THE SANCTITY OF LIFE AND STILL SUPPORT THE DEATH PENALTY? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT MAY CHALLENGE BOTH SIDES
paragraphs: CAN YOU DEFEND THE SANCTITY OF LIFE AND STILL SUPPORT THE DEATH PENALTY? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT MAY CHALLENGE BOTH SIDES

If every human life bears the image of God, why does Scripture permit the taking of life as punishment? And if Jesus died to save sinners, how should Christians respond when a sinner deserves the severest judgment? This is not merely a debate about criminals and punishment. It is a confrontation with justice, mercy, the Cross, and the uncomfortable truth about our own hearts.
Imagine receiving a phone call that changes your life forever.
Someone you love has been murdered.
Not in an accident. Not through an unfortunate mistake. Someone deliberately took their life.
Your knees weaken. Your mind refuses to accept what you have heard. You reach for your phone, hoping someone will tell you it isn't true.
But it is.
Yesterday, that person had a voice. A smile. Plans for tomorrow. Perhaps a child waiting at home. Perhaps a mother who had been praying for their safety.
Today, there is an empty chair.
And somewhere, the person responsible is still breathing.
Now imagine standing in a courtroom, listening as the evidence reveals exactly what happened.
The cruelty. The suffering. The final moments.
The judge announces that the crime is punishable by death.
Would you support that sentence?
Before you answer, consider another scene.
A condemned prisoner sits alone in a cell. He has committed a terrible crime. He cannot undo what he did. His victim will never return to their family.
But one night, he opens a Bible.
For the first time in years, he begins to weep.
Not because he has been caught.
Because he finally understands the weight of his sin.
He falls to his knees and cries out to Jesus Christ for mercy.
And the Gospel declares that even a murderer who truly repents is not beyond the saving power of the blood of Jesus.
Now the question becomes painfully complicated.
If God can forgive him, should the government still execute him?
If we believe every human being bears God's image, can we support capital punishment?
And if we oppose capital punishment, are we ignoring the justice God Himself established?
Here is what makes this question so difficult: Scripture confronts both the person who demands punishment without mercy and the person who speaks of mercy while overlooking the seriousness of evil.
We cannot settle it with a slogan.
We must open the Word of God.
And we must be willing to let Scripture correct us, even when it challenges what we already believe.
The first truth we must establish is that human life is sacred.
Not because people are innocent.
Not because people are useful.
Not because people have earned the right to exist through good behavior.
Human life has extraordinary dignity because human beings are created in the image of God.
Genesis 1:27 declares:
"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים — be-tselem Elohim, meaning "in the image of God."
This is not a declaration that human beings are divine. It means that humanity possesses a God-given dignity and calling unlike anything else in creation.
And here is something we cannot afford to miss.
The image of God is not erased simply because someone commits a terrible crime.
A murderer remains morally accountable before God precisely because he is a human being responsible for his actions.
His sin does not make him innocent.
But neither does it make him something less than human.
That distinction matters.
Because the moment we begin treating human beings as worthless objects, even when they are guilty, we risk forgetting whose image they bear.
Yet the very next biblical passage many Christians cite in defense of capital punishment is rooted in that same sacredness of human life.
Genesis 9:6 declares:
"Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man." (KJV)
Read that again.
The verse does not present human life as cheap.
It presents human life as so valuable that the deliberate shedding of innocent blood calls for the gravest accountability.
The Hebrew reads:
שֹׁפֵךְ דַּם הָאָדָם בָּאָדָם דָּמוֹ יִשָּׁפֵךְ
Shofekh dam ha-adam, ba-adam damo yishafekh.
A close rendering is:
"Whoever sheds human blood, by a human shall his blood be shed."
The wording is part of God's covenantal instructions to Noah after the flood, before the establishment of Israel's Mosaic law.
This is one reason many Christians believe capital punishment can be consistent with the sanctity of life.
Their reasoning is not necessarily that criminals have no value.
It is that murder is such a profound violation of human dignity that the state may impose the ultimate penalty.
But notice something important.

Genesis 9:6 establishes the seriousness of bloodshed. It does not provide a complete modern criminal justice system. It does not explain contemporary standards of evidence, wrongful convictions, appeals, corruption, or whether every government should exercise the maximum punishment available to it.
Those questions require further biblical and moral reasoning.
And Scripture gives us more to consider.
Under the law given to ancient Israel, certain offenses were punishable by death.
Exodus 21:12 states that a person who strikes another so that he dies is subject to death.
But the same chapter distinguishes intentional murder from an unintentional killing, providing for refuge in appropriate circumstances (Exodus 21:12–14).
Numbers 35:30 also requires multiple witnesses before a murderer may be put to death.
And Deuteronomy 17:6 rejects execution on the testimony of a single witness.
These provisions reveal something deeply significant.
Even where Scripture authorized capital punishment, it did not treat the taking of life as something to be done carelessly.
There were distinctions.
There were evidentiary requirements.
There was a recognition that guilt had to be established rather than assumed.

We must also remember that ancient Israel's covenant laws were given to a particular nation under a particular divine arrangement. Christians disagree about which judicial principles carry forward directly into modern civil government.
We cannot simply lift every penalty from the Mosaic law and demand its implementation today while ignoring the broader covenantal context.
Then we arrive at the New Testament.
And the discussion becomes even more searching.
Romans 13:1–4 describes governing authorities as accountable to God for maintaining public order and punishing wrongdoing.
Paul writes that the ruler "beareth not the sword in vain" (Romans 13:4, KJV).
The Greek expression is:
οὐ γὰρ εἰκῇ τὴν μάχαιραν φορεῖ
Ou gar eikē tēn machairan phorei.
A close translation is:
"For he does not bear the sword without purpose."
The Greek word μάχαιρα — machaira refers to a sword or large knife, a weapon that could symbolize coercive authority and the ability to use deadly force.
Many Christian interpreters understand this passage as recognizing the state's authority to impose severe punishment, potentially including capital punishment.
But we must be careful.
Paul does not explicitly command every government to execute murderers. Nor does the mere mention of the sword establish that every use of state power is just.
Romans 13 recognizes legitimate governing authority. It does not declare that governments are incapable of corruption.
The same Bible that calls believers to respect lawful authority also records rulers who murdered the innocent, abused their power, and condemned righteous people.
And that brings us to a scene that should make every Christian tremble before speaking too confidently about the death penalty.
Jesus Christ Himself was sentenced to death by human authorities.
Think about that.
The only perfectly innocent human being who ever lived was condemned through a profoundly unjust process.
Religious leaders pursued His destruction.
Political authority failed to protect the innocent.
The crowd demanded His death.
And the Roman governor, despite recognizing the weakness of the accusations, handed Him over to be crucified.
Luke 23:4 records Pilate saying:
"I find no fault in this man." (KJV)
Yet Jesus was still executed.
The Cross exposes the terrifying possibility that a legal system can possess the power to kill without possessing the justice to use that power rightly.
A government can issue a sentence.
A court can announce a verdict.
A crowd can applaud.
And an innocent person can still die.
That does not automatically prove that all capital punishment is immoral.
But it permanently destroys the illusion that human institutions are incapable of catastrophic error.
And unlike imprisonment, execution cannot be reversed.
An innocent prisoner may one day walk free.
An executed innocent person cannot be restored to earthly life by a corrected verdict.
This is one of the strongest reasons Christians who affirm the sanctity of life may oppose the death penalty, even while believing that murder deserves severe punishment.
They are not necessarily denying justice.
They are asking whether fallible governments should possess an irreversible power when their judgments can be wrong.
And that question becomes even more serious in societies where wealth, influence, discrimination, inadequate legal representation, unreliable evidence, or corruption can affect criminal proceedings.
If the powerful can escape punishment while the poor face execution, are we witnessing biblical justice?
Or are we witnessing something Scripture repeatedly condemns?
Proverbs 17:15 declares:
"He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD." (KJV)
God condemns both failures.
Acquitting the guilty.
And condemning the innocent.
Biblical justice cannot be reduced to punishment alone.
It must also concern truth, impartiality, integrity, and protection against wrongful judgment.
But there is another side of this conversation that deserves equal seriousness.
What about the victims?
What about the families whose lives have been shattered?
What about the child who will never see her father again?
What about the mother who must bury her son because someone deliberately murdered him?
Christians must never use the language of grace to silence the suffering of victims.
Forgiveness does not mean that murder was a minor offense.
Mercy does not require pretending that evil was harmless.
And compassion for a convicted murderer must never become indifference toward the people whose lives were destroyed.
The God of Scripture hears the cries of the oppressed.
He cares about the vulnerable.
He hates injustice.
Psalm 9:9 describes the Lord as a refuge for the oppressed.
And Revelation 6:10 portrays the martyrs crying out for God's righteous judgment.
The desire for justice is not inherently sinful.
Sometimes it is a response to something genuinely evil.
But there is a line between seeking justice and surrendering our hearts to vengeance.
And Scripture warns us not to cross it.
Romans 12:19 declares:
"Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord." (KJV)
Interestingly, this instruction appears immediately before Paul's discussion of governing authority in Romans 13.
That context matters.
Paul distinguishes personal retaliation from the public responsibility of civil government.
A Christian may believe that the state has authority to punish while also believing that private vengeance is forbidden.
Yet a Christian may also conclude that the state should exercise its authority through secure imprisonment rather than execution.
These positions differ on the proper exercise of civil power, but neither should be caricatured as automatically rejecting biblical justice.
Now consider the moment when Jesus was confronted with people demanding a woman's death.
In John 8:1–11, the account of the woman caught in adultery presents an extraordinary confrontation between accusation, sin, and mercy.
Jesus says:
"He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." (John 8:7, KJV)
One by one, the accusers depart.
Then Jesus tells her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (John 8:11, KJV)

We should note that this passage has a well-known textual history: the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John do not contain it, and many modern Bibles mark it accordingly. Its message should therefore be considered alongside the wider, securely attested teaching of Scripture.
We must also avoid misusing the account.
It is not a straightforward judicial ruling abolishing every form of capital punishment.
The situation concerns adultery, not murder, and involves serious questions about the accusers and their application of the law.
But the account powerfully illustrates a truth consistent with Jesus' wider ministry.
He did not minimize sin.
He confronted it.
Yet He also exposed self-righteousness and extended mercy.
"Go, and sin no more."
Not, "Your sin never mattered."
Not, "There is no such thing as accountability."
But an invitation to leave sin behind.
Grace is not permission to continue in evil.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that calls sinners into a transformed life.
And nowhere is that truth more startling than at Calvary.
There were three men hanging on crosses that day.
Two were criminals.
One was the sinless Son of God.
One criminal joined in the mockery.
But the other came to recognize something that changed everything.
He acknowledged his own guilt.
He admitted that his punishment was deserved.
And he recognized the innocence of Jesus.
Luke 23:41 records his words:
"And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss." (KJV)
Then he turned toward Jesus.
Not with an impressive religious record.
Not with years of good works.
Not with the opportunity to repair everything he had broken.
He had nothing left to offer.
Only a dying confession.
And a desperate plea.
"Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." (Luke 23:42, KJV)
Jesus answered:
"Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." (Luke 23:43, KJV)
Do not miss what happened.
The criminal was not rescued from earthly execution.
He was rescued from condemnation before God.
His repentance did not erase the earthly consequences of his actions.
But the mercy of Christ reached him even in his final hours.
The Cross reveals that forgiveness before God and consequences under human law are not the same thing.
A person can be genuinely forgiven by God and still face imprisonment.
A murderer can truly repent and still owe restitution wherever restitution is possible.
A criminal can receive eternal life through Jesus Christ without becoming innocent of the earthly crime committed.
And yes, a person facing execution can be saved by grace through faith.
That is not an endorsement of every death sentence.
It is a declaration that no human punishment possesses the power to cancel the saving promise of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is greater than a prison cell.
Greater than a courtroom verdict.
Greater than a criminal record.
Greater even than the approaching hour of death.
But here is the question that should haunt every one of us.
If the thief on the cross had been your child's murderer, would you still rejoice that Jesus offered him paradise?
That is not an easy question.
It is not meant to shame grieving families.
No one should demand that a victim's loved ones instantly feel forgiveness or abandon their pursuit of lawful justice.
But it confronts something deep within the human heart.
We love the idea of grace when we are the ones who need it.
We sometimes struggle with grace when it reaches someone who has wounded us.
And yet the Gospel does not belong to us.
We do not decide who is beyond the reach of Christ.
Consider the apostle Paul.
Before he became a missionary, he persecuted the church.
Acts 8:1 records his approval of Stephen's killing.
Acts 9:1 describes him breathing out threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord.
Later, Paul remembered his former life with deep humility.
In 1 Timothy 1:15, he wrote:
"Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief." (KJV)
God did not excuse Paul's persecution.
He confronted him.
He transformed him.
And He used the very man who had once terrorized Christians to proclaim the Gospel of grace.
This does not mean every criminal will repent.
It does not mean every profession of faith is genuine.
And it does not mean a dangerous offender should automatically be released.
But it does mean that no Christian should casually declare another person spiritually irredeemable.
We do not possess God's perfect knowledge of a human heart.
Only God can judge repentance without error.
And that leads to a distinction too often forgotten in public debates.
The question of whether the death penalty is morally permissible is not identical to the question of whether it is wise, just, or necessary for a particular government to use it.
A Christian may believe Genesis 9 and Romans 13 establish the moral legitimacy of capital punishment in principle, while opposing its use in a country with unreliable courts.

Another Christian may believe the sanctity of life, the possibility of repentance, the example of Jesus, and the danger of wrongful execution provide compelling reasons to reject the practice altogether.
Another may support its use only for the most extreme cases of intentional murder, with exceptionally strong safeguards.
These positions cannot simply be declared equally correct on every point.
They involve real disagreements about biblical interpretation, moral responsibility, the authority of the state, and the application of justice.
But Christians should recognize that thoughtful believers who submit to Scripture have reached different conclusions.
The Bible explicitly condemns murder.
It explicitly affirms human dignity.
It explicitly recognizes a role for civil authorities in punishing wrongdoing.
It explicitly forbids personal vengeance.
It explicitly calls God's people to justice and mercy.
And it explicitly proclaims forgiveness through Jesus Christ to repentant sinners.
What it does not provide is a single detailed New Testament policy prescribing how every modern nation must legislate capital punishment.
We should therefore be cautious about claiming more certainty than Scripture itself establishes.
And we should be especially cautious about declaring that anyone who disagrees with us on the death penalty must be an unfaithful Christian.
Our convictions should be strong enough to withstand honest examination.
And our humility should be deep enough to recognize where faithful interpretation requires careful judgment.
But perhaps the most dangerous thing in this entire debate is not the disagreement itself.
Perhaps it is what the disagreement can reveal about our hearts.
Because it is possible to support the death penalty while secretly enjoying the thought of another person's suffering.
And that is not justice.
It is possible to oppose the death penalty while showing little concern for victims and their families.
And that is not biblical compassion.
It is possible to quote Romans 13 while ignoring governmental corruption.
It is possible to quote John 8 while refusing to acknowledge the seriousness of sin.
It is possible to defend the sanctity of life in public while speaking of certain human beings as though they were disposable.
And it is possible to speak passionately about mercy while withholding it from the people closest to us.
The problem is not always that we lack Bible verses.
Sometimes the problem is that we have learned to use Bible verses to defend conclusions without allowing God's Word to examine our motives.
So before asking whether a Christian can support the death penalty, perhaps we should ask something more personal.
When you imagine a murderer standing before a judge, what do you want most?
Justice?
Protection for the innocent?
Truth?
Repentance?
Or simply the satisfaction of watching someone suffer?
There is a difference.
God is just.
But He is not cruel.
God is merciful.
But He is not indifferent to evil.
Exodus 34:6–7 reveals the Lord as merciful and gracious, while also declaring that He does not simply leave guilt unaddressed.
The God of the Bible is not divided between an angry Old Testament and a loving New Testament.
He is the same holy God.
His justice and mercy are not competing personalities.
They are revealed together in His righteous character.
And nowhere do we see that more clearly than at the Cross of Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
He did not announce that evil no longer mattered.
The Son of God bore our sins.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
"But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." (KJV)
Romans 3:25–26 presents Christ's sacrifice as the demonstration of God's righteousness, showing how God can be just and the justifier of the one who believes in Jesus.
The Cross is not a picture of justice being abandoned.
It is the place where God's holiness, love, righteousness, and mercy are revealed through the saving work of Christ.
Jesus was not an unwilling victim of the Father's cruelty.
He willingly gave His life in obedience to the Father for the redemption of sinners.
John 10:18 records Jesus saying:
"No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself." (KJV)
And the resurrection declares that death did not have the final word.
This is why Christians must be careful not to confuse the Cross with an ordinary criminal execution.
Jesus' death was a unique, voluntary, redemptive sacrifice by the sinless Savior.
No modern government can reproduce it.
No condemned criminal can atone for the sins of humanity.
And no execution carried out by the state possesses the power to save a soul.
Only Jesus saves.
So where does that leave us?
Can a Christian support the death penalty while believing in the sanctity of life?

Yes, a Christian can hold those convictions together, if the support for capital punishment is grounded in a serious understanding of human dignity, legitimate civil authority, proportionate justice, and the protection of the innocent—not hatred, cruelty, or revenge.
That position has biblical arguments deserving careful consideration.

But a Christian can also oppose the death penalty precisely because human life is sacred, governments are fallible, wrongful execution is irreversible, and the state may be able to protect society through other severe penalties.
That position also has substantial biblical and moral arguments deserving careful consideration.
The more important question is whether our convictions have been shaped by the whole counsel of Scripture or merely by the verses most convenient to our position.
Do we care about innocent lives before a crime happens?
Do we care about victims after a crime happens?
Do we care about fair trials?
Do we care about prisoners who may truly repent?
Do we care about the families of those who are executed?
Do we care about the possibility that an innocent person may be condemned?
Do we care about protecting society without allowing hatred to shape our hearts?
And above all, do we care about honoring Jesus Christ more than winning an argument?
Because the Christian calling is not merely to take a position.
It is to become more like Christ.
Micah 6:8 declares:
"He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" (KJV)
Justice.
Mercy.
Humility.
Not justice without mercy.
Not mercy without truth.
Not moral confidence without humility.
And not religious language without love.
Perhaps you are reading this as someone who has lost a loved one to violence.
You may be carrying grief that other people cannot comprehend.
You may be angry.
You may be exhausted by a justice system that seems painfully slow.
You may have heard Christians tell you to forgive before anyone has even acknowledged the depth of what happened.
Please hear this.
Your loved one's life mattered.
Their death matters.
Your grief matters.
The Lord does not command you to call evil good.
And seeking lawful accountability does not make you less Christian.
Healing may be long and difficult. Forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation, and it does not eliminate the need for safety, boundaries, or justice.
Jesus sees the pain that other people cannot see.
Psalm 34:18 reminds us:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." (KJV)
And perhaps you are reading this from the other side.
Maybe you have done something terrible.
Maybe you have harmed someone.
Maybe you have destroyed relationships, betrayed trust, or committed a sin you cannot undo.
You cannot escape responsibility by simply saying that God forgives.
True repentance turns away from sin, tells the truth, and accepts the responsibility that follows.
But do not believe the lie that you are beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
The same Savior who heard the dying thief can hear you.
The same Lord who confronted Paul can transform you.
The same grace that rescued sinners throughout Scripture is still sufficient for everyone who comes to Christ in genuine repentance and faith.
Your past may carry consequences.
But it does not have to remain the master of your soul.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
From Scandal to Grace. Because Jesus Rewrites Everything.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because grace makes evil acceptable.
Not because forgiveness erases every earthly consequence.
But because the risen Christ can take a life ruined by sin and begin a transformation no human court could ever accomplish.
And now, I want to ask you something that requires more than a quick reaction.
After reading the Scriptures, where do you stand?
Do you believe capital punishment can be a legitimate expression of justice?
Do you believe the sanctity of life calls Christians to oppose it?
Or are you still wrestling with the tension between justice, mercy, and the possibility of wrongful judgment?
You do not have to pretend to have every answer.
If you are still wrestling, you can simply comment, "Lord, teach me justice and mercy."
If this article has exposed bitterness, a desire for revenge, or a lack of compassion in your own heart, you can pray, "Jesus, change my heart."
You do not owe anyone the details of your suffering.
Let the conversation become a place where people seek truth without cruelty and practice compassion without compromising conviction.
Because perhaps someone reading the comments is a grieving parent.
Perhaps someone is a prison chaplain.
Perhaps someone has a loved one serving a life sentence.
Perhaps someone is struggling to believe that God could ever forgive what they have done.
Your words, spoken with humility and truth, may help someone take one more step toward Jesus.
Not to provoke an argument.
Not to embarrass people who disagree.
But because our world desperately needs conversations about justice that do not forget mercy, and conversations about mercy that do not abandon truth.
One thoughtful share may reach someone who would never enter a church or open a Bible on their own.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have drifted from the faith, and even those who are still searching for God to follow along.
Because spiritual growth does not happen merely by collecting inspirational quotes.
It happens as the Holy Spirit works through God's Word, calling us to repentance, faith, obedience, and deeper communion with Jesus Christ.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped strengthen your faith, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading and sharing.

It is a practical way of standing alongside a ministry committed to proclaiming Jesus Christ, teaching Scripture, encouraging wounded hearts, calling sinners to repentance, and helping believers grow in biblical understanding.
It should not be confused with a required biblical tithe to a local church, nor should it replace your responsibilities to your family or your faithful support of your local congregation.

But if you believe this work is bearing good fruit, and God has given you the ability and desire to support it, your generosity can help make more Scripture-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to others.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the kind of support we value.
Not pressured giving.
Not guilt-driven giving.
But cheerful, voluntary partnership in Gospel ministry.
These items are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
They are simply an additional way of expressing gratitude to those who help sustain the work.
That commitment matters.
Because the Gospel must never be placed behind a price tag.
Pray for the ministry.
A faithful prayer, a compassionate conversation, or a shared Gospel message can be a meaningful act of service.
Because the goal has never been to build a following for its own sake.
The goal is to point people to Jesus Christ.
And as we close, return with me one final time to Calvary.
Three crosses.
Two guilty men.
One innocent Savior.
One criminal mocked Him.
The other asked for mercy.
And Jesus made a promise that death itself could not cancel.
That scene does not answer every legal question surrounding capital punishment.
But it answers something infinitely more important.
It tells us that even when earthly justice has reached its final sentence, the saving mercy of Jesus Christ is still powerful enough to reach a repentant sinner.
It tells us that human guilt is real.
That God's judgment is righteous.
That grace is undeserved.
And that the crucified and risen Savior is mighty to save.
So whether you support or oppose the death penalty, never forget the truth that stands above the debate.
The murderer is accountable before God.
The victim is precious before God.
The judge is accountable before God.
The government is accountable before God.
And every one of us will ultimately stand before the One who judges with perfect righteousness.
That should make us humble.
That should make us careful.
That should make us merciful.
And that should drive us to the Cross.
Because when we look at Calvary, we discover something none of us should ever forget.
The most important question is not simply whether a guilty person deserves to die, but whether any of us could stand before a holy God without the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The answer is no.
And the hope of the Gospel is that we do not have to.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
And everyone who truly turns to Him in repentance and faith can receive forgiveness and eternal life.
Justice matters.
Life matters.
Truth matters.
Mercy matters.
But above everything else, Jesus Christ is Lord.
And when the arguments are over, when the courtroom has emptied, when the headlines have disappeared, and when every earthly verdict has become part of history, one truth will remain:
The Cross reminds us that the only perfectly innocent Man ever executed willingly gave His life so that guilty people like us could be forgiven.
